A law-enforcement systematic review and meta-analysis is retained as review-level, provisional sleep and work-stress context [16].

In a prospective military cohort, cardiorespiratory fitness was evaluated in relation to physiological responses and dropout during a loaded long-distance march [13].

A firefighter crossover study found no statistically or clinically significant cardiometabolic or fire-ground performance effect from four weeks of astaxanthin; most inflammatory changes were within treatment groups [17].

In a Slovenian infantry sample, end-running speed, maximal heart rate, and predicted VO2max from the 30-15 intermittent fitness test had test-retest ICCs of .971, .960, and .975, respectively, and the authors reported validity and usefulness against treadmill and 2-mile run measures [5].

In a military training cohort of 1,407 trainees assessed before and after eight weeks, DXA and circumference data were collected for body-composition comparison [10].
A firefighter Tactical Athlete Resilience Program reported feasibility outcomes, not definitive effectiveness [11].
A separate firefighter pilot investigation reported training outcomes but requires replication and controlled effectiveness testing [14].
A retrospective tactical-athlete cohort reported associations of sex, military occupation, and rank with anterior cruciate ligament injury risk [12].
A cross-sectional study of Swedish soldiers reported occupational exposure and musculoskeletal-complaint associations [15].

The concept-mapping work with 48 participants identifies priorities created by recruits, police staff, health professionals, and researchers [6].

In a prospective cohort of 724 police recruits from 15 Massachusetts academies (661 graduates and 63 non-graduates), lower entry-level muscular-endurance and aerobic-fitness performance was associated with higher odds of academy non-graduation after adjustment for age, sex, and body mass index: OR 9.6 (95% CI 3.5–26.3) for ≤15 versus 41–60 sit-ups, OR 6.7 (95% CI 2.5–17.5) for ≤20 versus 41–60 push-ups, and OR 18.4 (95% CI 6.8–50.2) for a >15 min 20 s versus 10 min 37 s–12 min 33 s 1.5-mile run [21].
A second recruit cohort found that push-up capacity and estimated VO2max from run time predicted successful academy graduation in its reported models [22].

In a small prospective observational study of a five-day specialist tactical police selection course, 18 male candidates started and 11 completed the course; two self-withdrew and five were medically withdrawn [24].

Among completers, body mass (−2.05 kg, p=0.006), right-hand grip strength (−14.48 kg, p<0.001), left-hand grip strength (−14.27 kg, p<0.001), and sit-and-reach flexibility (−6.64 cm, p<0.001) decreased significantly across the selection week, whereas the reported power output, peak jump velocity, and vertical-jump-height outcomes did not show statistically significant deterioration [24].
The IsoKai lift-test study contributes reliability and agreement information for Swedish Armed Forces admission testing [28].

Neurocognitive scores in several memory, attention, and speed domains were lower on the day after nighttime work, whereas some domains were exceptions and adjusted analyses retained design-specific qualifications [23].
The caffeine-plus-theacrine tactical-personnel study is retained as contextual information about an acute, physically fatiguing setting [26].
The ice-slurry study reported lower estimated sweat volume per body mass under its beverage condition while several physiologic and subjective outcomes did not differ during exercise [25].
The cooling review summarizes heterogeneous outdoor occupational interventions [27].
